title: Australia and Turkey criticised for hosting COP31 while supporting coal
content:
Australia and Turkey, the co‑hosts of the upcoming United Nations climate conference COP31, are being criticised by activists for their continued involvement in the coal supply chain and for not outlining a clear plan to abandon fossil fuels. Global campaign group 350 Org has called on the two nations to announce a definitive coal phase‑out date and to provide national roadmaps for moving away from coal, gas and oil.

The criticism comes as the COP31 summit approaches, scheduled to take place in the Turkish Mediterranean city of Antalya in about a month. Activists say the hosts have created a “vacuum of action” on transition plans, a key objective for many participating countries.
summary: Turkey and Australia, the hosts of the upcoming COP31 climate conference in Antalya, are being criticised by activists for their role in a coal supply chain and for remaining largely silent on a global fossil‑fuel transition. Campaign group 350.org has urged the two countries to announce a coal phase‑out date and national roadmaps for moving away from coal, gas and oil before the summit.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Over 1,200 Colorado students earn climate ‘seal’ in statewide program
content:
More than 1,200 Colorado students have earned a climate “seal” through a statewide initiative that pairs climate‑focused coursework with community service, a program that is now expanding to other states.  

The initiative requires participants to combine classroom learning about climate issues with hands‑on projects that benefit their local communities.  

At Vista Academy, a charter school near Denver’s main airport, student Anthony Muñoz partnered with a local university to create a garden of native plants that can detect ground‑level ozone pollution. He also collaborated with climate scientists from the National Center for Atmospheric Research in Boulder, who guided him on data collection, interpreting leaf conditions for air‑quality insights, and the importance of milkweed for monarch butterfly migration.
summary: More than 1,200 Colorado students have earned a climate ‘seal’. The seal is awarded through a statewide initiative that pairs climate‑focused coursework with community service, such as student Anthony Muñoz’s garden project at Vista Academy guided by National Center for Atmospheric Research scientists.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Brain study finds irrelevant visual details hinder decisions under uncertainty
content:
New brain research indicates that irrelevant visual details can interfere with decisions made under uncertainty. The study highlights how such extraneous information disrupts the decision‑making process.

Cognitive flexibility—the capacity to adjust thinking or behavior as situations change—is known to decline gradually with age and in conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, schizophrenia and substance use disorders. One component of this flexibility involves the ability to switch between tasks without becoming distracted or losing focus.
summary: Brain research shows that irrelevant visual details can interfere with decisions made under uncertainty. Cognitive flexibility, which includes the ability to switch tasks without distraction, tends to decline with age and in conditions such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, schizophrenia and substance use disorders.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Polyubiquitin may help stabilize tau filaments in Alzheimer's disease
content:
New research indicates that polyubiquitin could help stabilize tau filament structures that accumulate in neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s disease.  

In affected brains, progressive neuronal damage is linked to the buildup of abnormal tau filaments. The filament core forms a highly ordered structure, while ubiquitin molecules are attached to tau around this core as post‑translational modifications.  

Although ubiquitin’s presence on the filament periphery is documented, the specific contribution of these modifications to the structural stability of tau filaments remains unclear. The study’s findings suggest that polyubiquitin may play a stabilizing role, warranting further investigation.
summary: Abnormal tau filaments accumulate in the brains of patients with neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's, causing progressive neuronal damage. Researchers suggest that polyubiquitin attached to tau around the filament core could contribute to the structural stability of these filaments, though its precise role remains unclear.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Weekly cisplatin fails to show fewer serious side effects in p16-negative head and neck cancer
content:
Weekly cisplatin fails to show fewer serious side effects in p16‑negative head and neck cancer.  

Physicians typically treat locally advanced head and neck cancer with either a higher dose of cisplatin given every three weeks or a lower dose given weekly in combination with radiation.  

Before the NRG‑HN009 trial, there was limited randomized evidence to determine which regimen provided the best balance of cancer control and treatment‑related side effects.
summary: Physicians typically use either a higher dose of cisplatin given every three weeks or a lower dose given weekly in combination with radiation to treat locally advanced head and neck cancer. However, before NRG-HN009, there was limited randomized evidence to determine which regimen provided the best balance of cancer control and treatment-related side effects.
author: Medical Xpress

title: E. L. F. Beauty releases album “Mirror Mix” as it ramps up marketing spend
content:
Brands are increasingly turning to original music as part of their marketing strategies.  

E. L. F. Beauty released an album titled “Mirror Mix” and said the brand will increase its marketing spend for the remainder of the year.  

The music release illustrates how companies are using creative content to boost visibility.
summary: E. L. F. Beauty released an album titled “Mirror Mix”. The brand plans to increase its marketing spend for the rest of the year.

title: Chick-fil-A aims to remain family-owned while expanding internationally
content:
Chick‑fil‑A is pursuing growth while maintaining its family‑owned identity, according to the company’s latest statements. The fast‑food chain plans to expand further in the United States and abroad, yet emphasizes that its family‑business roots will remain intact.

Under the leadership of CEO Andrew Cathy, Chick‑fil‑A has been entering new international markets. The company is also broadening its menu offerings, adding new items to appeal to a wider customer base.

The firm’s expansion strategy is being carried out with a focus on preserving its family‑business culture, as noted by the company’s leadership.
summary: Chick-fil-A is expanding into new international markets and growing its menu under CEO Andrew Cathy. The company says it wants to remain a family business as it expands in the U.S. and abroad.
author: CNBC Business

title: Hungarian paprika growers Nikoletta and Laszlo Pajsan battle Europe's driest summer
content:
Hungary's dwindling paprika producers are fighting to preserve a staple of the country's culinary heritage. Farmers Nikoletta Pajsan Nagy and Laszlo Pajsan are among those battling the effects of Europe’s driest summer on their red pepper crops.

Working from before dawn until midnight, the Pajsan farmers have been laboring to save their harvest in Hungary, confronting the severe drought conditions that threaten the viability of their paprika production.
summary: Farmers Nikoletta Pajsan Nagy and Laszlo Pajsan worked from before dawn until midnight. They fought Europe's driest summer ever to save their red pepper harvest in Hungary.
author: Phys.org

title: Wavefront shaping uncovers correlations via giant light fluctuations in opaque media
content:
Researchers have reported that giant fluctuations of focused light reveal hidden correlations in opaque materials.  

When light propagates through a strongly scattering material—such as biological tissue or other disordered opaque media—it follows many different paths and generates a seemingly random speckle pattern. Wavefront shaping enables control of this complex interference, allowing the light to be focused through the material.  

The observed giant fluctuations in the focused light indicate the presence of underlying correlations within the scattering medium.
summary: Light traveling through strongly scattering materials such as biological tissue follows many paths and creates a random speckle pattern. Wavefront shaping can control this interference to focus light, producing giant fluctuations that reveal hidden correlations in opaque media.
author: Phys.org

title: Inka sacrificial llamas at Tambo Viejo found with coca leaves stuck in wool
content:
Archaeologists working at the ruins of Tambo Viejo in Peru’s Acarí Valley have found coca leaves still attached to the wool of sacrificed llamas, indicating that the Inka scattered the sacred plant over the animals during ritual offerings.  

The site, identified as an Inka provincial center, has previously yielded tasseled sacrificial llamas and brightly adorned guinea pigs, but evidence of coca’s role in ceremonies had been scarce. The newly discovered leaves provide direct material proof of how the plant was incorporated into Inka ritual practice.  

The find adds a tangible element to the understanding of Inka religious customs involving coca, a plant long regarded as sacred in Andean culture.
summary: Excavations at the Inka provincial center of Tambo Viejo in Peru's Acarí Valley uncovered sacrificial llamas with tassels and brightly adorned guinea pigs. Archaeologists also found coca leaves still attached to the wool of some of the sacrificed llamas.
author: Phys.org

title: UCLA study links specific gut bacteria to faster brain aging and cognitive decline
content:
A study conducted by researchers at UCLA has found a connection between the composition of gut bacteria and the rate of brain aging. The investigation identified specific gut microbes and their chemical byproducts as markers linked to faster brain aging.

Individuals whose brains appeared older based on the study’s measures also showed poorer performance in memory, focus and mood assessments. The researchers noted that these biological signs of brain aging can emerge decades before noticeable cognitive or emotional symptoms.

The findings raise the possibility that the gut could become a target for interventions aimed at preventing or slowing brain aging, although further research is needed to confirm this potential approach.
summary: A UCLA study found that faster brain aging is linked to specific gut bacteria and their chemical byproducts. The study also observed that brains appearing older were associated with poorer memory, focus and mood, indicating biological signs may appear decades before symptoms and could eventually make the gut a target for prevention.
author: Science Daily

title: 30-year Australian forest experiment finds heavy thinning yields large trees, carbon gains
content:
A 30‑year forestry experiment in Australia has produced an unexpected outcome, according to the study’s findings.  

The trial showed that mountain ash forests subjected to heavy thinning grew unusually large trees and recovered enough carbon to match or exceed the levels measured in untouched forest areas.  

Researchers say the results suggest that carefully managed thinning could simultaneously support timber production, wildlife habitat and carbon storage.
summary: A 30-year forestry experiment in Australia found that heavily thinned mountain ash forests grew unusually large trees. The thinned forests also recovered enough carbon to match or exceed untouched areas, suggesting careful thinning could support timber production, wildlife habitat, and carbon storage simultaneously.
author: Science Daily

title: Oklahoma meteor crater dated to 370 million years, 100 million years younger than thought
content:
A meteor crater buried beneath Oklahoma has been dated to be almost 100 million years younger than earlier estimates.  

Analysis of zircon crystals indicates the Ames impact occurred about 370 million years ago, overturning the previous view that it was part of the Ordovician bombardment once associated with a hypothesized ring of debris around Earth.  

The revised age places the impact in close temporal alignment with a major mass extinction that devastated marine life.
summary: Zircon crystals show the Ames impact occurred about 370 million years ago, making the buried Oklahoma crater nearly 100 million years younger than scientists previously thought. Instead, the impact coincided closely with a major mass extinction that devastated marine life.
author: Science Daily

title: Diet soft drinks match water for weight loss in two-year trial of 493 adults
content:
A two‑year randomized clinical trial found that diet soft drinks are essentially as effective as water for long‑term weight loss and weight maintenance.  

The study enrolled 493 adults with overweight or obesity and assigned participants to drink either beverages sweetened with aspartame, acesulfame‑K or sucralose, or plain water. Both groups lost a similar amount of weight over the trial period.  

In addition to comparable weight loss, participants in each group experienced reductions in waist size, improvements in body composition and several metabolic measures.
summary: A two-year randomized clinical trial of 493 adults with overweight or obesity found diet soft drinks were essentially as effective as water for long-term weight loss and maintenance. Both groups also saw improvements in waist size, body composition and several metabolic measures.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists say early magnetic fields could explain universe expansion discrepancy
content:
Scientists say that tiny magnetic fields generated shortly after the Big Bang could provide a clue to the persistent discrepancy in measurements of the universe’s expansion rate.  

Detailed simulations indicate that these primordial magnetic fields may have altered the formation of hydrogen in the early universe. The change in hydrogen formation would affect the cosmic microwave background, which in turn influences the expansion rate inferred from that background radiation.  

The findings suggest that the magnetic fields might help reconcile the long‑running disagreement over how fast the universe is expanding.
summary: Tiny magnetic fields created shortly after the Big Bang may help explain the long-running disagreement over how fast the universe is expanding. Simulations indicate these primordial fields could have altered early hydrogen formation, affecting the cosmic microwave background and the expansion rate inferred from it.
author: Science Daily

title: Global detectors report substantial geoneutrino measurements mapping Earth's interior
content:
Elusive “geoneutrinos” are now helping scientists create a new map of Earth’s volatile interior.

A global network of detectors has reported some of the most substantial measurements yet of neutrinos generated deep underground. These neutrinos are produced by radioactive elements that power the planet’s tectonic activity. The data provide a clearer view of the processes occurring within Earth’s interior.
summary: A global network of detectors is reporting some of the most substantial measurements yet of neutrinos created deep underground. Those neutrinos are produced by radioactive elements that power the planet’s tectonic activity.

content:

content:

title: Portable MP3 players see collapse and resurgence, covered in The Stepback newsletter
content:
The Stepback newsletter, a weekly tech‑world digest, focuses on the collapse and resurgence of portable media players. The story is highlighted by Terrence O’Brien, who provides deeper insight into the rise, fall, and rise of MP3 players.

Subscribers receive the newsletter each Sunday at 8 AM ET, and the publication invites new readers to opt in for future issues.

Portable digital music first appeared in 1998 with the advent of the MP3 player. Prior to that, people carried booklets of CDs on the bus or a handful of cassettes in their backpacks. The full story is available on The Verge.
summary: The Stepback weekly newsletter breaks down the collapse and resurgence of portable media players. It is authored by Terrence O'Brien and arrives in subscribers' inboxes on Sundays at 8 AM ET.

title: Google's First Chromebook, the Cr-48, Was a Conceptual Prototype, Not a Marketed Product
content:
The Verge’s latest episode of Version History revisits the origins of Google’s ChromeOS, focusing on the company’s first prototype, the Cr‑48. The Cr‑48 was never marketed as a consumer product and carried no distinctive design or logos, according to the show. Instead, it served as a proof‑of‑concept that introduced the idea of a web‑centric operating system.

In the episode, hosts Nilay Patel of The Verge and Marques Brownlee (MKBHD) sit down with David Pierce to trace the evolution of ChromeOS and Chromebooks. They discuss whether Google’s hardware strategy was the right one and how the Cr‑48 paved the way for later devices.

The episode is part of a season of Version History that has examined iconic school technology. The previous installment covered Nicholas Negroponte.
summary: Google’s first Chromebook, the Cr-48, was not marketed as a product and had no distinctive design or logos. In a recent Version History episode, Nilay Patel, Marques Brownlee, and David Pierce discussed ChromeOS history and the merits of Google's hardware strategy.
author: The Verge

title: iPad Mini $100 off during Amazon Prime Big Deals Days
content:
Apple’s iPad Mini is temporarily on sale for its old price ahead of Amazon’s October Prime Big Deals Days. Both Wi‑Fi only and cellular‑connected models are $100 off.

The Wi‑Fi version with 128 GB of storage is currently $499, the 256 GB model is $599, and the cellular model with 128 GB of storage is $649. This base configuration of the tablet often sold for around $400 throughout 2025, so the current price is the best since late June. A new version later this year could be significantly more expensive.

The 2024 iPad Mini is the seventh‑generation model, featuring Apple’s A17 Pro chip and support for Apple Intelligence. It is compatible with the Apple Pencil Pro and offers faster Wi‑Fi and USB‑C speeds. A review of the launch noted the processor upgrade and Apple Intelligence features, but also that the tablet lacked some quality‑of‑life improvements found in the larger iPads released at the same time.
summary: Apple’s iPad Mini is $100 off ahead of Amazon’s October Prime Big Deals Days, with the Wi‑Fi 128 GB model priced at $499, the 256 GB Wi‑Fi model at $599, and the 128 GB cellular model at $649. The discount is the lowest price for the tablet since late June.

title: Apple MacBook Air M5 gets $200 discount on Amazon during Prime Day
content:
Amazon’s October Prime Day has brought the first price cut in months for Apple’s 2026 MacBook Air (M5).  The 13‑inch model, which normally sells for $1,299, is now $1,099, a $200 discount.  The 15‑inch version, normally $1,499, is listed at $1,299, also a $200 reduction.

Both the 13‑inch and 15‑inch Airs ship with 512 GB of storage and the new M5 chip.  The larger model adds two extra speakers for a total of six and two additional GPU cores, improving overall graphical performance.  The 13‑inch Air is noted as being faster than Apple’s $699 MacBook Neo.

Apple’s 2026 MacBook Air (M5) features a faster processor and storage, long battery life, a bright display, and excellent speakers.  The sale represents the first price drop for the Air in several months.
summary: The 13‑inch MacBook Air with the M5 chip and 512 GB storage is priced at $1,099 on Amazon, down from its usual $1,299. The 15‑inch model with the same storage is listed for $1,299 on Amazon, reduced from $1,499.

title: AirPods Pro 3 drop to $179 on Amazon during October Prime Day
content:
Apple’s AirPods Pro 3 are now available for $179 on Amazon during the October Prime Day sale, down from the original $249 price. The discount marks the first time the earbuds have sold for less than $190 since the June Prime Day event. The deal includes the noise‑canceling model with five ear‑tip sizes, live translation, improved bass, and fairly accurate heart‑rate sensors.

While the AirPods 5 offer a lower price, the Pro 3’s enhanced fit, superior noise cancellation, and additional features make it a better value at $30 more. Other retailers are expected to follow Amazon’s pricing in the coming days.
summary: AirPods Pro 3 are being sold for $179 on Amazon, down from $249, as part of an October Prime Day discount. The earbuds include five ear‑tip sizes, live translation, superior noise cancellation, improved fit, better bass and heart‑rate sensors.
author: The Verge

title: IEA and climate negotiators aim to set electricity‑shift target for economy
content:
The International Energy Agency (IEA) and climate negotiators are pushing to establish a target that would shift the economy to run on electricity, according to recent discussions.

The proposed goal aims to accelerate electrification across sectors, reflecting the agencies’ focus on using electricity as the primary energy source for future economic activity.
summary: The IEA and climate negotiators want to set a target for shifting the economy to run on electricity. The goal is to transition economic activity to electricity.

title: Trump appoints DNI Jay Clayton as White House AI czar
content:
President Donald Trump on Sunday named Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to also serve as the White House AI czar.  

Clayton, who leads the United States’ 18 intelligence agencies, previously was the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan and headed the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump’s first term.  

During his Senate confirmation hearing for the DNI position, Calyton said AI was a “gamechanger” but also posed “a threat.”
summary: Donald Trump on Sunday named Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, as the new White House AI czar. Clayton leads the United States' 18 intelligence agencies and previously served as Manhattan's top federal prosecutor and head of the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump's first term.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Amsterdam neighbours sue over TikTok‑viral chip shop Fabel Friet's crowd impact
content:
Residents of one of Amsterdam’s most exclusive neighbourhoods have taken the city to court over the licensing of Fabel Friet, a chip shop on Runstraat that has gone viral on TikTok. At a hearing last week, neighbours described how the shop’s popularity has turned the narrow canal street into a congested thoroughfare.

On busy days the queue for Fabel Friet stretches across a bridge on the Keizersgracht, one of Amsterdam’s most famous canals, and tourists line the street seven days a week waiting for orders. The influx of visitors has been linked to increased litter, as well as the presence of gulls and rats loitering on parked cars, the street, steps and porches.
summary: Neighbours in an exclusive Amsterdam neighbourhood have taken the city to court over the licensing of Fabel Friet, a chip shop that went viral on TikTok. They say the shop’s queues clog Runstraat and the Keizersgracht bridge, attract litter, gulls and rats, and draw crowds of tourists seven days a week.
author: Guardian Technology

title: FlyDubai captain Smit Machchhar says he has ‘one more fight left’ after opening cockpit door
content:
FlyDubai captain Smit Machchhar said he had “one more fight left in me” after he managed to open the cockpit door during a violent incident.  

Machchhar recounted to Israeli prime minister Benjanim Netanyahu how the attack began and described opening the door after nearly losing his vision from repeated blows by the co‑pilot.
summary: FlyDubai captain Smit Machchhar told Israeli prime minister Benjanim Netanyahu how the attack began and how he opened the cockpit door. He said he nearly lost his vision from the co‑pilot’s repeated blows before finally opening the door.
author: Euronews

content:

title: Latvia's United List leads with 35.4% as vote count reaches 99.9%
content:
Latvia’s pro‑European ruling party, the United List led by Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, secured a victory in the parliamentary election, while populist parties made gains, according to the headline.  

State television reported that with more than 99.9 percent of votes counted, the United List was in the lead with 35.4 percent of the vote.  

The result confirms the United List’s leading position as the election nears its final tally.

title: Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro clash in Brazil presidential race
content:
Twelve candidates are on Brazil’s presidential ballot, but the contest is focused on two rivals: incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro. Lula is campaigning for a fourth and final term, warning that Brazil’s sovereignty is at stake amid pressure from Donald Trump.

Bolsonaro, positioning himself as a bridge to the United States, emphasized his ties to the White House and called for better U.S. deals, including on Brazil’s rare mineral resources. Commentary on the race comes from Nick Rushworth, who discusses the controversial senator, and Dr Andrea Aruska de Souza Santos, Director of the King’s College Brazil Institute in London, who provides additional insight.
summary: The election features twelve candidates but centers on President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro. Lula is seeking a fourth term and warns Brazil's sovereignty is at stake, while Bolsonaro emphasizes White House ties and calls for better U.S. deals on rare mineral resources.
author: France 24

title: Palestinians say army and settlers increase drone use in occupied West Bank
content:
Palestinians and activists say the use of drones in the occupied West Bank has risen sharply.  According to their reports, the drones are being operated by both the Israeli army and civilian settlers, to whom the government provides the equipment directly.  

The parties claim the unmanned aircraft are employed to intimidate residents, conduct surveillance, carry out demolitions and otherwise make daily life unbearable for Palestinians living in the area.
summary: Palestinians and activists report a rise in drone usage in the occupied West Bank, with the army and settlers receiving drones directly from the government. They say the drones are used to intimidate, monitor, demolish and make daily life unbearable.
author: France 24

title: Rwandan genocide suspect hunter Dafroza Gauthier dies at 72
content:
Rwandan genocide suspect “hunter” Dafroza Gauthier died at the age of 72 on Saturday in Reims, France.  

For almost three decades, Gauthier and her husband Alain tracked down Rwandan refugees in France who were suspected of participating in the 1994 Tutsi genocide. Their work focused on bringing to justice those allegedly responsible for the massacre that killed more than 800,000 people.  

Gauthier’s death marks the end of a career dedicated to pursuing accountability for the events of 1994.
summary: Dafroza Gauthier, who for nearly 30 years with her husband Alain tracked down Rwandan refugees in France suspected of participating in the Tutsi genocide, died in Reims on Saturday at age 72. She had dedicated her life to bringing to justice those allegedly responsible for the 1994 massacre of more than 800,000 people.
author: France 24

title: France to suspend lessons at up to 500 high schools on Monday amid student protests
content:
Up to 500 high schools across France are expected to have lessons “totally or partly suspended” on Monday, the education minister announced, citing ongoing student protests.  

The protests, which have been described as sometimes violent, target teacher shortages, dilapidated school buildings and overcrowding in classrooms.  Since the start of the demonstrations, the minister reported that 24 schools have been “burned or ransacked.”  

The closures will affect up to 500 schools, according to the minister’s statement.
summary: Lessons will be totally or partly suspended at up to 500 high schools across France on Monday, the education minister said. The minister added that 24 schools had been burned or ransacked since the protests began.
author: France 24

title: Yemen's leader launches counter‑offensive as Houthis block supply route to Taiz
content:
Yemen's leader announced on Sunday the launch of a major military operation against the Iran‑backed Houthis, with the goal of recapturing territory under their control.  

The announcement came as Houthi forces cut off a vital supply route to the besieged government‑held city of Taiz, according to several security sources.
summary: The leader of Yemen's Saudi‑backed government announced on Sunday the beginning of a major military operation against the Iran‑backed Houthis to recapture territory they control. Houthi forces cut off a vital supply route to the besieged government‑held city of Taiz, security sources said.
author: France 24

title: Lula da Silva seeks fourth term in Brazil's closely watched presidential election
content:
Brazilians began casting their votes on Sunday in a closely watched presidential election in which 80‑year‑old incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is seeking a fourth term.

title: New York production re-stages 1993 Larry Kramer and Anthony Fauci C-SPAN debate
content:
A New York production is re-staging a 1993 televised debate between Aids activist Larry Kramer and Anthony Fauci, then director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases. The original confrontation took place on November 30, 1993, on C-Span, a cable channel typically associated with congressional coverage rather than the high-intensity verbal exchanges seen on programs like CNN’s Crossfire. During the hour-long discussion, moderated by journalist Steve Scully, the two men clashed over the US government’s response to the Aids crisis, with Fauci asserting institutional legitimacy and Kramer arguing that institutions presiding over genocide lack it.

Scully attempted to keep the conversation focused on centrist concerns, primarily regarding money, while redirecting the pair when passions erupted. The broadcast also featured phone calls from civilians whose empathy and expertise in Aids varied widely. Although the segment was described as an exhausting hour that settled little, it demonstrated the dynamic of people yelling at each other loudly enough to be heard while also listening. The new production aims to bring this "extraordinary hour" to life as a masterclass of controlled fury.
summary: A New York production re-stages the 1993 C-SPAN debate between Aids activist Larry Kramer and Anthony Fauci, director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases. The event featured journalist Steve Scully moderating the two men as they argued about the US government's response to the Aids crisis.

title: ‘Brave from the beginning’: 20 years of Friday Night Lights – the sports drama that dared to be different
content:
The sports drama Friday Night Lights marked its 20th anniversary, having launched the careers of Jesse Plemons and Michael B. Jordan while allowing its cast to improvise in a fresh manner. The series, set in small-town Texas, depicted the intense cultural significance of high school football in communities where the outcome of Friday night games defined the local mood for days.

Britt Daniel, the frontman of the Texas band Spoon, noted the show’s authenticity by comparing its setting to his hometown of Temple, which he described as very similar to the fictional town of Odessa. Daniel recalled that in such towns, everything centered around the Friday football game, and he experienced significant social tension and physical threats during his youth. He stated that residents had to look over their shoulder in public spaces like malls, parking lots, and parties because people were eager to fight.
summary: It launched the careers of Jesse Plemons and Michael B Jordan, and let its stars improvise in a way that was fresh and new. This show about smalltown US football was confident, trailblazing – and wonderfulI’ve been around the south of the US enough to have seen the importance of football: little burgs where the high-school football field has stands that wouldn’t disgrace a League Two soccer club in the UK.

title: Lamine Yamal stars again as Spain see off Czechia and maintain perfect start
content:
Spain secured a 3‑1 victory over Czechia in Oviedo, extending their perfect start to the Nations League and keeping them a single point from the quarter‑finals. Teenager Lamine Yamal opened the scoring within six minutes, marking the third consecutive game in which he netted early. The goal, described by Spain’s manager Luis de la Fuente as a sign that Yamal is “on course to become a legend,” helped Spain complete their World Cup homecoming.

After a 2‑0 halftime lead—thanks to a second goal from Rodrigo Hernández—Spain substituted Yamal. Czechia, however, rallied in the second half, with Jiri Slama scoring on 69 minutes. In the 79th minute, a potential equaliser from Ryan Naderi was ruled out by referee Vassilis Fotias for a foul on Robin Le Normand, as the free‑kick that led to the attempt was swung in. Spain’s win leaves them a point away from the Nations League quarter‑finals.
summary: Lamine Yamal scored twice in Spain's 3-1 win over Czechia in Oviedo, keeping Spain a point from the Nations League quarter finals. Spain's manager Luis de la Fuente praised Yamal as a future legend, while Czechia's late comeback attempt was denied by referee Vassilis Fotias.

summary: A research team from KAIST says that when members feel securely accepted in a group, they can express dissenting opinions in greater detail and more persuasively. title: Human tau seeds trigger disease-specific shapes in mouse brains
content:
A new study reveals that human tau seeds induce disease-specific shapes within mouse brains. Tau is a protein naturally present in the brain, where it plays an essential role in proper neuron development and facilitates communication between neurons.

When this protein becomes misshapen or misfolded, it can drive the progression of neurodegenerative diseases. The abnormal buildup of tau is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, and scientists have also linked misfolded tau to more than 20 other neurodegenerative conditions.
summary: A new study found that human tau seeds trigger disease-specific shapes in mouse brains. Misfolded tau, a protein essential for neuron development, is associated with Alzheimer's and more than 20 other neurodegenerative diseases.

content: A four-year research initiative focused on mapping the complete protein profile of mitochondria in parasites responsible for sleeping sickness, giardiasis, leishmaniasis, and babesiosis has identified ancient pathways and dozens of potential new drug targets. The study was driven by the critical role mitochondria play as the "powerhouse of the cell," with researchers noting that disrupting this energy production halts the parasite's function. These four diseases collectively impact nearly one billion people annually.

title: Atmospheric momentum exchange alters Earth rotation under global warming
content:

While the mechanism of this momentum exchange is not a new concept, researchers are investigating the specific effects that occur under conditions of long-term global warming.
summary: Atmospheric circulation carries angular momentum and can exchange it with the solid Earth to slightly alter the planet's rotation rate. The article investigates how this process occurs under long-term global warming.

title: Physicists Find Topological Wave Knots in Materials That Resist Imperfections
content: Physicists have identified topological properties in certain materials and devices, characterized by wave behaviors that resemble knots in a rope. These properties are defined by whole numbers that remain unchanged despite small imperfections, much like a knot persists through stretching or twisting until the rope is cut. This robustness against defects and noise has established topology as a central concept in modern physics, offering potential for the development of resilient electronics, photonics, and quantum devices.
summary: Physicists have found that some materials and devices carry topological properties in how waves move through them. These properties, labeled by whole numbers that do not change under small imperfections, promise electronics, photonics, and quantum devices that tolerate defects and noise.

title: New Study Finds Unknown Brain Circuit Linked to OCD
content:
Treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), a mental health condition defined by distressing, uncontrollable thoughts and repetitive behaviors, has traditionally relied on psychotherapy and medication to manage symptoms. New research has identified a previously unknown brain circuit involved in the condition.

This discovery could serve as a key step toward developing treatments that target specific brain regions, potentially allowing for better control of OCD.
summary: A study has identified a previously unknown brain circuit involved in obsessive‑compulsive disorder. This discovery could lead to treatments that target specific brain regions to better control the condition.

title: Menopause is a major health milestone, yet health records barely track it—new research
content:
A recent study has highlighted that menopause, a major health milestone for anyone with ovaries who lives long enough, is rarely documented in medical records.  

The research notes that menopause is a natural transition in midlife that can strongly affect a person's quality of life and increase their current and future risk of heart disease, osteoporosis, and other health issues.  

Given these significant health implications, it is notable that whether someone is experiencing or has gone through menopause is seldom recorded in their medical records.
summary: Anyone with ovaries who lives long enough will experience menopause. Medical records do not consistently reflect whether a person is experiencing or has gone through menopause, despite its impact on quality of life and risk of heart disease, osteoporosis, and other issues.

title: Injectable Foam Prototype Could Seal Deep Wounds and Prevent Amputations
content:
Injectable foam prototype could seal deep wounds and help prevent amputations

A new prototype uses a caulking gun filled with silicone compound to allow doctors and nurses to seal deep wounds caused by blast injuries. The device is intended for future use in clinical settings.

By sealing such wounds, the technology aims to prevent amputations and reduce mortality among patients with severe injuries.
summary: A caulking gun filled with silicone compound will allow doctors and nurses to seal deep blast‑injury wounds. This could prevent amputations and reduce mortality for patients with severe wounds.
